dimensions.reasons: Group B zephyranthes_white_flower clearly shows the requested central white six-petaled flower with a pale green center, yellow anthers, and surrounding strap-like leaves against a blurred earthy ground. The overall macro-flower subject is recognizable.
issues: The petals are broad, rounded, and very uniform rather than the reference's tapered pointed lanceolate tepals.
The target's fine longitudinal petal venation and clearly legible yellow-green throat are largely absent.
Group A views reveal the apparent ground is a small square texture tile with circular cutouts on a large plain brown plane, not a coherent natural litter bed.
The submitted scene includes simplified foliage and ambiguous pink capsule-like objects not present in the reference.

dimensions.reasons: The petals and floral center are assembled into a recognizable bloom, and the leaves cluster near it. However, the Group A side, wide, and top views show a very thin, panel-like soil surface with exposed circular holes and a large underlying plane.
issues: No convincing supporting stem or attachment of the flower head to the ground is visible.
The soil is visibly a thin square tile rather than continuous terrain.
Large circular notches expose the underlying floor and undermine the physical plausibility of the outdoor scene.
Several rigid leaves appear laid across or emerging from the flower area without convincing botanical connections.

dimensions.reasons: The essential color coding is present: white petals, a light green center, yellow anthers, green leaves, and brown ground. The flower silhouette reads immediately as a six-petaled bloom in Group B.
issues: Petal silhouettes have bulbous rounded ends rather than the pointed star-like form of the reference flower.
Petals are nearly featureless pure white surfaces, with no clearly visible fine vein pattern.
Leaves are thick, smooth, and simplified compared with natural narrow strap foliage.
The green-to-white throat transition is weak and visually overwhelmed by the bright petals.

dimensions.reasons: The render contains some photographic cues such as blurred background foliage and textured ground in Group B, but the focal flower itself is visibly overexposed and simplified.
issues: The author final image is severely washed out: most petal surface detail and shading are lost.
The shallow depth of field does not produce a crisp, readable flower comparable to the sharp reference bloom.
Group A exposes artificial staging, including the isolated terrain tile, cutouts, flat surrounding plane, and purple environment.
The flower and foliage read more as clean stylized geometry than as a coherent natural macro photograph.

dimensions.reasons: The final image places the flower centrally in a high, slightly inclined macro-like view, with leaves diagonally around and behind it, broadly echoing the reference composition.
issues: The leaves are concentrated heavily toward the right and lower-left instead of creating the reference's more naturally distributed diagonal background framing.
The central bloom is extremely flat and radially regular, whereas the reference has more varied petal angles and a more pronounced bowl-like throat.
In Group A wide views, the flower is tiny relative to the oversized square ground tile and surrounding staging plane.

dimensions.reasons: Within the close author render, the six petals, central reproductive structures, and leaves have a generally understandable relative scale.
issues: The petals are disproportionately broad and paddle-like for the intended rain-lily-like flower.
The yellow anthers and pale pistil are very small and insufficiently prominent for a teaching-oriented botanical close-up.
The evaluator wide views make the flower look miniature relative to its excessively large ground tile.
The leaves appear unusually thick and chunky relative to the bloom.

dimensions.reasons: There is an attempt at soft focus and a warm natural-earth palette, while the ground texture includes visible litter-like variation in Group A.
issues: A harsh concentrated bright patch in Group A and extreme exposure in Group B blow out the white petals.
Petal translucency, waxy highlight response, and longitudinal normal-map veins are not visibly resolved.
The yellow-green throat does not read as a clear controlled gradient into white petals.
Leaves lack convincing fine texture or restrained natural gloss, and the lighting does not resemble the balanced soft daylight of the reference.

dimensions.reasons: The submission visibly includes a single six-petaled white bloom, a green throat area, multiple yellow-tipped stamens, a pale central pistil, strap leaves, and an earthy ground treatment. These cover the major requested object categories.
issues: Fine petal veins, a clearly readable throat gradient, and crisp educational visibility of the floral center are missing or obscured by overexposure.
The required dry leaf-and-woodchip litter is replaced largely by a textured soil/creeping-plant tile.
A supporting stem is not clearly visible.
Extra pink oblong objects and the tile cutouts are unexplained additions not appropriate to the requested small natural scene.

criteria.criterion: The principal flower must form a complete six-tepal body with the required shape, venation, and material response.
The flower throat must use an authored spatial gradient that produces a clearly readable yellow-green-to-white instructional color transition.
The complete stamen, anther, and pistil system must have the specified identities, arrangement, material response, and unobstructed instructional visibility.
The surrounding living leaves must combine the requested form, distribution, direction, color, and surface response.
criteria.evidence: The close final render and cam_submitted view show several predominantly green, elongated pointed strap leaves extending diagonally behind and beneath the flower, with a soft restrained highlight rather than metallic reflectance.

criteria.criterion: Dry fallen leaves and wood chips must jointly form a substantial, materially varied organic ground bed.
The authored key and environmental fill must work together to produce soft natural daylight and photographic shadows.
The final image must combine the requested elevated-oblique macro view, shallow focus, subject hierarchy, and broad reference character.
criteria.evidence: The exported final image has a close elevated view and blurred surroundings, but the white flower is strongly overexposed: the petal surfaces and their required fine resolution are washed out rather than crisply resolved. The blind description likewise identifies heavy washout and depth-of-field blur obscuring petal and ground detail.

criteria.criterion: The completed vignette must maintain plausible biological scale, avoid invented modeled structures and unrelated objects, and integrate into a coherent instructional scene.
criteria.evidence: The multi-view renders reveal the flower placed on a very thin square textured ground panel with several large circular cutouts, surrounded by a separate dark-brown plane and purple environment. These exposed staging structures, together with ambiguous pink oblong objects behind the leaves and an unclear flower support, make the scene read as a disconnected modeled assembly rather than one coherent natural macro vignette.

criteria.criterion: The editable Blender project must correspond to the final scene, preserve the required authored render configuration, produce a clean result, and use organized naming.
The designated final image must be a valid authored PNG at the required effective resolution.

notes: The core white six-petaled flower is recognizable and has basic stamens, pistil, leaves, and ground context. However, it is substantially less faithful than the reference: rounded featureless petals, weak throat and vein detail, blown-out lighting, simplified foliage, and visibly artificial tiled ground staging prevent it from serving as a convincing botanical macro reconstruction.
score_policy: Frozen paper score: uncapped 0.5 rubric + 0.5 dimension.
